title: Written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34)
hook: I will write my law in their hearts

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah's letter and the word shalom, and your line was pray for your city. What did you do for the place you live? Day four hundred seventy-six.

Think of something you know by heart. Not something you looked up. Something that's just in you. Your phone number from childhood. The words to a song you haven't heard in twenty years. A grandmother's recipe you make without measuring. The Lord's Prayer, maybe, or a psalm. You don't consult it. You don't need the paper. It comes up out of you, even at three in the morning. That's a very different kind of knowing from a rule posted on a wall. Jeremiah, in the darkest days before Jerusalem fell, heard God promise that kind of knowing. Today, the covenant written on the heart.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU KNOW BY HEART.` → `NOT ON PAPER. IN YOU.` → `A DIFFERENT KIND OF KNOWING.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah." A covenant is a binding relationship, sealed with promises on both sides, like a marriage more than a contract. The covenant at Sinai was written on stone tablets. And the people, Jeremiah says, broke it, though God had been like a husband to them. So what's new? "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people." Same God. Same people. Same law, the Hebrew word is torah, teaching. But written in a new place: not on stone, on the heart. And then: "they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them." No one will need to teach a neighbor to know the Lord. Even the least. And the deepest promise of all: "I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more." Here, readers differ, and it matters to say it carefully. Jewish readers hear a promise to Israel: the same covenant, renewed and finally taken to heart. Christians hear it fulfilled in Jesus: at the Last Supper he speaks of the cup as the new covenant in his blood, and the letter to the Hebrews quotes this whole passage. The very name New Testament comes from this phrase, through the Latin word for covenant. This week we've walked through the servant, the thirsty, good news to the poor, a prophet too young, the potter, the city's peace, and now: the heart.
screen: `A COVENANT: A BINDING RELATIONSHIP.` · `NOT ON STONE, ON THE HEART.` · `ALL SHALL KNOW ME, THE LEAST TOO.` · `NEW TESTAMENT MEANS NEW COVENANT.` · then, large: `I WILL WRITE IT IN THEIR HEARTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: start learning one good thing by heart. Settle, and breathe. Choose something short: a verse, a line of a prayer, the psalm you picked to keep this year, or simply today's line, I will write it in their hearts. Say it slowly in your mind. Then again, without looking. Then again, more slowly. Notice which words slip away and which stay. Don't rush. You're not memorizing for a test. You're letting something move from the page into you. If you pray, you can pray the words as you learn them. The bell holds the time.
New covenant. Jeremiah's promise of God's teaching written on the heart, not stone, with sins forgiven and remembered no more.
Your line: on the heart. Today, say your chosen words three more times, at breakfast, at noon, at bedtime, until you don't need to look. Day four hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Christians hear the new covenant named at every communion service, in the words over the cup; many also memorize scripture, and Jeremiah 31:31–34 is read in Lent and at services focused on forgiveness.

fork.setup: the old covenant is broken, and the city is about to fall. what does God promise through Jeremiah?
options: a stricter law, carved deeper into stone.
his law written on their hearts.
an end to any covenant at all.
fork.reveal: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts." not tougher stone. a different place to write.

original.note: Hebrew: a new covenant. the phrase appears only here in the Hebrew Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: new covenant is a Christian term for the New Testament.
what it means: Jeremiah's promise that God's teaching will be written on the heart, every person will know God, and sin will be forgiven.
what a scholar hears: berit chadashah, found only here in the Hebrew Bible. the Greek diatheke became the Latin testamentum, and so the New Testament got its name.
